title: Doro Wat
subtitle: ethiopian spiced chicken stew
excerpt: Ethiopia's richest slow-cooked stew, built on deeply caramelised onions and a warming spice blend. Whole eggs are added at the end and simmered until just set.
sourceNotes: Doro Wat is Ethiopia's national dish, traditionally prepared for celebrations and holidays including Ethiopian Christmas.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the stew without the eggs for up to three months. Add boiled eggs when reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Scales well. Use a large stockpot if doubling.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The stew improves overnight. Reheat gently and add a splash of water if it thickens too much.

glossaryTerms.definition: Ethiopia's national dish, a rich slow-cooked chicken stew spiced with berbere blend.

content.text: begins with a long, slow cook of onions in dry heat, with no oil added until they are almost paste-like. This step is what gives the stew its deep, sweet base. Patience here makes the difference between a good result and a great one.
The spice blend draws on chilli, cardamom, cinnamon and allspice. Hard-boiled eggs added near the end absorb the sauce and are the dish's most iconic feature.

items.prepNote: hard-boiled, peeled, scored with a fork

content.text: Place the grated onions in a dry dutch oven over medium heat. Cook, stirring often, for 20 to 25 minutes. The onions should reduce to a thick, dark paste. Do not add oil yet.
Add the butter and stir to combine. Cook for another 5 minutes. Add the garlic, ginger, chilli flakes, paprika, coriander, cumin, allspice, cardamom and cinnamon. Stir constantly for 3 minutes.
Stir in the tomato puree and cook for 2 minutes. Add the chicken pieces and turn to coat in the sauce. Pour in the chicken stock and bring to a gentle simmer.
Cover and cook over low heat for 40 minutes, turning the chicken halfway through. The sauce should be thick and deeply coloured. Add a splash of water if it looks dry.
Nestle the scored eggs into the sauce. Spoon sauce over them and simmer uncovered for 10 minutes. Serve over injera or with rice.

attrs.issue: Onions are burning before they soften

content.text: Lower the heat and add a tablespoon of water. Stir more frequently. The goal is slow caramelisation, not frying.

attrs.issue: Sauce is too thin after cooking

content.text: Remove the lid and simmer over medium heat for 10 minutes to reduce. Doro Wat should coat the back of a spoon.
Increase the chilli flakes and add a small squeeze of lemon. Check that your spices are fresh. Old ground spices lose impact quickly.

Doro Wat is served at Ethiopian weddings and at the celebration of Genna, Ethiopian Christmas. It is always eaten with injera. The long dry-fry of onions is a uniquely Ethiopian technique. It appears across the country's stew tradition, from lentils to lamb. No other cuisine quite does it the same way.
